To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Adolescent girls are more likely to be stunting and underweight than their male peers, but more likely to be overweight than boys.
adolescent boys are at a higher risk of stunting and underweight but lower risk of overweight/ obesity and PHH compared to their female counterparts.
adolescent boys were more likely than girls to have stunting, underweight, and pre-hypertensive or hypertensive status, while girls were more likely than boys to be overweight or obese.
In summary, our research is concerned with
adolescent health, nutrition, and hypertension.

the health and nutritional status of adolescent boys and girls in Ghana, and the factors associated with the risk of being stunted, underweight, overweight/obese, and pre-hypertensive/hypertensive (PHH).
the association between malnourishment, hypertension and sex among adolescent boys and girls aged 15– 19 years in Ghana.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the risk of malnutrition, PHH and their correlates are sex-differing among adolescents.
malnutrition and hypertension risk are sex-specific in adolescents.
malnutrition, hypertension risk, and their correlates are different for adolescent boys and girls in Ghana.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is an urgent need for a more comprehensive and gender-sensitive approach in adolescent nutrition interventions in Ghana.
adolescent boys and girls in Ghana are at risk of the double burden of malnutrition and the up-coming NCD burden.
the risk factors for malnutrition and hypertension are sex-specific.

adolescent health and nutrition interventions must be tailored to the needs of both sexes and that the sex differences in malnourishment and PHH are likely due to the different social and environmental factors that affect the two sexes.
